scripts.title: Amazing Facts That Sound Fake
lines: Get ready — fifteen facts that sound like magic, but every single one is true.
An octopus has three hearts, and two of them stop beating when it swims.
Honey never spoils — pots found in ancient Egyptian tombs were still good to eat.
Sea otters hold hands while they sleep, so the waves cannot carry them away.
A teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh about a billion tons.
Bananas are very slightly radioactive, because they are full of potassium.
The footprints astronauts left on the Moon can stay there for millions of years.
A blue whale's heart weighs as much as a small car.
Cows have best friends, and they get stressed when they are separated.
The first oranges were not orange at all — they were green.
A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance, and they are born grey, not pink.
Scientists found your nose can tell apart more than a trillion different smells.
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water — it is called the Mpemba effect.
There are more possible chess games than atoms in the whole universe.
That was only the beginning — the ocean hides even stranger secrets, coming next.

scripts.title: Giants of the Ocean
lines: The biggest animal that ever lived is still swimming in our oceans today.
The blue whale can grow longer than two buses parked in a line.
Its heart alone weighs as much as a small car.
A blue whale's tongue weighs as much as a whole elephant.
Whale songs can travel hundreds of kilometres through deep ocean water.
Humpback whales blow bubble nets to trap hundreds of fish at once.
A sperm whale's brain is the largest brain of any animal on Earth.
Whales sleep with only half of their brain at a time, so they never stop breathing.
The bowhead whale can live for more than two hundred years.
Whale falls feed whole cities of deep-sea creatures for decades.
A blue whale baby drinks hundreds of litres of milk every single day.
Some whales migrate farther than any other mammal on the planet.
Killer whales are actually the largest members of the dolphin family.
A whale's earwax grows in layers that record its whole life story.
The giants are gentle, ancient, and still full of mysteries.

scripts.title: Secrets of the Sharks
lines: Sharks were swimming in Earth's oceans before trees even existed.
A shark can lose tens of thousands of teeth in its lifetime — new ones always grow.
Sharks have a sixth sense that can feel the electricity of a beating heart.
The whale shark is a shark as big as a bus, yet it eats tiny plankton.
Great white sharks can leap completely out of the water to catch a seal.
Some deep-sea lantern sharks really do glow in the dark.
A shark's skeleton is made of cartilage, the same bendy stuff as your ears.
Greenland sharks move so slowly they are called the sleeping sharks.
The Greenland shark can live for around four hundred years.
Sharks existed before the dinosaurs — and survived every mass extinction.
A hammerhead's wide head gives it almost complete vision all around.
Tiger sharks are called the dustbins of the sea because they eat almost anything.
Sharks cannot swim backwards — their fins only push them forward.
A shark's skin feels like sandpaper and helps it swim faster.
Humans kill far more sharks than sharks ever harm humans — they need our protection.

scripts.title: The Power of Volcanoes
lines: Right now, about twenty volcanoes are erupting somewhere on Earth.
Volcano lava can flow hotter than one thousand two hundred degrees.
The biggest volcano in our solar system is Olympus Mons, on Mars.
Olympus Mons is about three times taller than Mount Everest.
In 1816, one eruption led to a year with no summer around the world.
Volcanic ash is not soft like snow — it is crushed rock and glass.
Underwater volcanoes build brand new islands from the sea floor.
A new island was born near Tonga in 2015, and scientists watched it grow.
Pompeii was buried in one day when Mount Vesuvius erupted in the year 79.
Much of the Earth's crust was built by volcanoes over billions of years.
Kilauea in Hawaii is one of the most active volcanoes on Earth.
Lightning can flash inside a volcano's ash cloud during an eruption.
Some volcano lakes are bright turquoise, coloured by minerals and gases.
After eruptions, volcanic soil becomes some of the richest farming land on Earth.
Volcanoes destroy, but they also create — land, islands, and life.

scripts.title: The Honey Bee Kingdom
lines: A single bee colony can hold sixty thousand bees — and one queen.
The queen bee can lay up to two thousand eggs in a single day.
Worker bees are all female, and they do every job in the hive.
A bee visits about fifty to a hundred flowers on one trip.
To fill one jar of honey, a colony flies thousands upon thousands of kilometres.
Bees talk by dancing — the waggle dance points the way to flowers.
The dance tells other bees both the direction and the distance.
A honey bee's wings beat about two hundred times every second.
Bees can see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that humans cannot see.
Honey never spoils — sealed pots stayed sweet for thousands of years.
Bees pollinate about one out of every three bites of food we eat.
When a bee finds a rich flower patch, she rushes home to share the news.
In winter, bees cluster together and shiver to keep the hive warm.
A bee's sting protects the colony — she gives her life for her sisters.
Protect the bees, and you protect the gardens of the whole world.

scripts.title: The Octopus Genius
lines: The octopus might be the smartest escape artist in the whole ocean.
An octopus has three hearts pumping blue blood through its body.
Two hearts push blood to the gills, and one serves the rest of the body.
When an octopus swims, the main heart stops — swimming tires it out.
With no bones, an octopus can squeeze through any gap its beak fits through.
Octopuses can change colour and skin texture in the blink of an eye.
They are masters of camouflage, matching rocks, sand, and coral.
Each octopus arm has its own mini-brain — most neurons live in the arms.
An octopus can taste with its arms as it explores.
Octopuses open jars and solve mazes to win their dinner.
Some octopuses carry coconut shells to use as portable armour.
The blue-ringed octopus is tiny, beautiful, and dangerously venomous.
A mother octopus guards her eggs without eating, until her last days.
Octopus ink does more than hide them — it also dulls a predator's sense of smell.
Eight arms, three hearts, one remarkable mind.

scripts.title: Earth of Extremes
lines: Our planet holds records that no other known world can match.
The hottest place ever recorded is Death Valley, at fifty-six point seven degrees.
The coldest place is Antarctica, where it fell below minus eighty-nine degrees.
Mount Everest grows a few millimetres taller every year.
The Mariana Trench could swallow Everest with kilometres to spare.
The largest desert on Earth is not the Sahara — it is Antarctica.
The Sahara is the world's largest hot desert, almost as big as the United States.
The Nile and the Amazon are the longest rivers on Earth, thousands of kilometres long.
Lightning strikes Earth about one hundred times every single second.
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on the planet.
It is so large that it can be seen from space.
Lake Baikal in Siberia holds about a fifth of the world's fresh lake water.
The Dead Sea is so salty that swimmers float like corks.
Iceland grows a little wider every year as tectonic plates pull it apart.
From burning deserts to frozen poles, Earth is a planet of extremes.

scripts.title: Mysteries of the Moon
lines: The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth, every single year.
It moves away by about four centimetres annually — about as fast as fingernails grow.
The Moon was probably born when a Mars-sized world crashed into the young Earth.
Moon dust smells like burnt gunpowder, the astronauts said.
There is no wind on the Moon, so footprints can last for millions of years.
The Moon has earthquakes too — scientists call them moonquakes.
A day on the Moon lasts about twenty-nine Earth days.
The same side of the Moon always faces Earth — the far side stayed hidden until 1959.
The Moon's gravity is so weak you could jump six times higher there.
Twelve astronauts have walked on the Moon — all between 1969 and 1972.
Neil Armstrong's first steps on the Moon were watched by millions on Earth.
The flag on the Moon needed a horizontal pole, because there is no wind to wave it.
Astronauts left mirrors on the Moon that still bounce laser beams back to Earth.
The Moon helps create the tides that rise and fall on our beaches.
During a total solar eclipse, the Moon covers the Sun almost perfectly.
That perfect fit is a cosmic coincidence of size and distance.
The dark patches on the Moon are ancient seas of frozen lava.
Early astronomers called them maria, the Latin word for seas.
The Moon has mountains taller than many on Earth.
Water ice hides in the shadowed craters near the Moon's poles.
Temperatures on the Moon swing from boiling days to freezing nights.
The Moon shines by reflected sunlight — it makes no light of its own.
A supermoon looks bigger because the Moon is closer to Earth in its orbit.
The Moon illusion makes it look giant near the horizon — a trick of your brain.
Robots from several nations now explore the Moon alongside orbiters.
India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023.
NASA's Artemis program plans to send astronauts back to the Moon.
Future astronauts may live in shielded bases near the polar ice.
The same Moon watched over the dinosaurs millions of years ago.
And one day soon, new footprints will join the old ones on its dust.

scripts.title: Secrets of the Jungle
lines: The jungle is the loudest, wildest classroom on Earth.
A jaguar's bite is so strong it can crush the skull of its prey.
Jaguars love water and are excellent swimmers, unlike most cats.
The poison dart frog is tiny, bright, and one of the most poisonous animals alive.
Some rainforest frogs carry their babies on their backs to pools in the treetops.
Howler monkeys are so loud, their calls carry for five kilometres.
The sloth moves so slowly that green algae grows in its fur.
That green fur works like camouflage among the leaves.
Leafcutter ants carry leaf pieces many times heavier than their own bodies.
Those ants do not eat the leaves — they farm fungus gardens underground.
The harpy eagle is one of the most powerful birds of prey in the world.
Its talons are as large as a grizzly bear's claws.
Toucans have huge beaks that are surprisingly light and hollow inside.
A toucan's beak also helps it cool down on hot days.
Capybaras, the largest rodents, are calm friends to almost every animal.
Spider monkeys use their tails like a fifth hand.
The glass frog is so transparent you can see its heart beating.
Anacondas can grow longer than a bus and swim silently through swamps.
Rainforest trees grow so tall they build a roof over the forest floor.
Some jungle plants trap and digest insects for food.
The rafflesia is the world's largest flower — and it smells like rotten meat.
Some jungle butterflies are almost as wide as a dinner plate.
A chameleon's tongue shoots out with stunning speed to snatch insects.
Chameleons can move each eye in a different direction at the same time.
The jungle at night fills with glowing fungi and shining eyes.
More than half of all plant and animal species live in rainforests.
Many medicines came from rainforest plants discovered by scientists.
Every minute, large areas of rainforest are at risk from cutting and fire.
Protecting the jungle protects the air of the whole planet.
The jungle never sleeps — it only changes its song.

scripts.title: The Deep Sea World
lines: Deeper than sunlight can reach, a hidden world glows in the dark.
The deep sea is the largest living space on planet Earth.
Anglerfish carry their own glowing fishing rod to hunt in darkness.
The female anglerfish is far bigger than the tiny male.
Some deep-sea fish make their own light — it is called bioluminescence.
The vampire squid is not a true squid at all — it is in a family of its own.
Giant squid have eyes as big as basketballs to catch the faintest light.
For centuries, sailors told tales of the kraken — the giant squid was real.
The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is tall.
At the bottom, the pressure could crush most submarines.
Yet shrimp and snailfish live happily even at those crushing depths.
The barreleye fish has a completely transparent head.
Its green eyes look upward through its own see-through skull.
Deep-sea corals can live for thousands of years in cold darkness.
Some deep corals are older than the oldest trees on land.
Black smokers on the sea floor blast water hot enough to melt lead.
Strange yeti crabs farm bacteria on their own hairy claws near hot vents.
The yeti crab waves its claws to grow gardens of bacteria for food.
A gulper eel's mouth is so huge it can swallow prey bigger than itself.
The tripod fish stands on the sea floor on three long fins.
Some deep fish have no scales and skin soft as jelly.
The fangtooth has the largest teeth of any fish for its size.
Snow falls in the deep sea too — white flakes of food from above, called marine snow.
Almost everything in the deep depends on that slow snowfall of food.
The oarfish, a ribbon longer than a bus, may have inspired sea serpent legends.
We have better maps of the Moon than of our own ocean floor.
Every deep dive discovers species nobody has ever seen before.
Robots and brave explorers now light up this dark world, metre by metre.
The deep sea guards Earth's climate by holding enormous amounts of carbon.
The darkest place on Earth may hold the brightest discoveries of all.

scripts.title: Stranger Than Fiction — Round Two
lines: Just when you thought facts could not get stranger — round two begins.
Wombat droppings are cube-shaped — yes, really.
Scotland's national animal is the unicorn.
Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal on Earth.
A shrimp's heart is located inside its head.
Slugs have four noses on their heads.
A blue whale's heartbeat can be picked up from kilometres away.
Polar bears have black skin under their white-looking fur.
Their fur is not white at all — it is translucent and hollow.
A crocodile cannot stick its tongue out.
Butterflies taste with their feet.
The dot over the letter i has its own name — it is called a tittle.
Australia is wider than the Moon.
Venus is the only planet that spins clockwise.
A bolt of lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Koalas have fingerprints almost identical to human fingerprints.
The unicorn may be Scotland's symbol, but narwhals are real sea unicorns.
An ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.
A day on Venus is longer than its whole year.
Sharks are older than trees — by tens of millions of years.
The inventor of the Pringles can is buried in one.
M and Ms were named after their two inventors, Mars and Murrie.
There is a species of fungus that turns ants into zombies.
Your body produces about twenty-five million new cells every second.
Humans and giraffes have the same number of neck bones — seven.
A group of owls is called a parliament.
The first person to survive going over Niagara Falls in a barrel was a sixty-three-year-old teacher.
Octopus arms can taste what they touch, without asking the brain.
The Moon is drifting away from us a little more every year.
Thirty facts later, the world is officially stranger than fiction.

scripts.title: The Great Space Voyage
lines: Tonight we travel farther than any human has ever gone — without leaving our seats.
Our journey begins with the Sun, a star so wide that a million Earths could fit inside it.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach your eyes.
So when you look at sunlight, you are looking into the past.
Mercury, the closest planet, races around the Sun in just eighty-eight days.
A year on Mercury is short, but a single day there lasts for months.
Venus is the hottest planet, wrapped in thick clouds of acid.
Venus spins backwards, so on Venus the Sun rises in the west.
Earth is the only world we know where oceans, forests, and life flourish.
From space, Earth glows blue — a tiny marble in endless black.
Our Moon is one of the largest moons compared to its planet.
Mars is red because its dust is full of rusted iron.
Mars hosts Olympus Mons, a volcano nearly three times the height of Everest.
Robots roam Mars today, drilling rocks and hunting signs of ancient water.
Ancient Mars once had rivers, lakes, and perhaps a great northern ocean.
Jupiter is the giant — more than eleven Earths could line up across it.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than planet Earth itself.
That storm has been raging for hundreds of years.
Jupiter's moon Europa hides an ocean beneath its shell of ice.
Scientists think Europa's hidden ocean could be a home for life.
Another moon, Ganymede, is even bigger than the planet Mercury.
Saturn's rings are made of countless pieces of ice and rock.
The rings are hundreds of thousands of kilometres wide, yet only about ten metres thick.
Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a giant ocean.
Saturn's moon Titan has lakes and rain — but of liquid methane, not water.
Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side like a giant barrel.
Uranus is the coldest planet, colder than minus two hundred degrees.
Neptune, the farthest planet, has the fastest winds in the solar system.
Winds on Neptune can race at two thousand kilometres per hour.
Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy worlds like Pluto.
Pluto, the beloved dwarf planet, has a heart-shaped glacier on its surface.
Comets are dirty snowballs that grow glowing tails near the Sun.
Halley's Comet visits us about every seventy-six years.
Asteroids are rocky leftovers from the birth of the planets.
One asteroid impact ended the reign of the dinosaurs sixty-six million years ago.
Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through a comet's dusty trail.
The International Space Station circles Earth every ninety minutes.
Astronauts on the station see sixteen sunrises every single day.
Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object, beyond the edge of the Sun's wind.
It still whispers data home across more than twenty billion kilometres.
The Milky Way is our home galaxy, with hundreds of billions of stars.
Our solar system takes over two hundred million years to circle the galaxy once.
At the galaxy's heart sits a black hole millions of times heavier than the Sun.
The nearest big galaxy, Andromeda, is on a slow collision course with us.
In about four billion years, the two galaxies will gracefully merge.
Astronomers have already found more than five thousand planets around other stars.
Some of those exoplanets may have oceans, clouds, and maybe life.
The James Webb telescope can see the light of the first galaxies ever formed.
That light travelled more than thirteen billion years to reach us.
The universe itself is about thirteen point eight billion years old.
Everything you have ever seen is made of atoms forged inside ancient stars.
In a very real way, we are all made of stardust.
Yet for all we have learned, most of the universe remains invisible and unknown.
Dark matter and dark energy together make up about ninety-five percent of everything.
Every telescope we build asks bigger questions than the last.
And every clear night, the whole universe waits above your roof, free to watch.
So the next time you look up, remember how far the story reaches.
The voyage never truly ends — it only waits for the next curious mind.

scripts.title: Animal Superpowers
lines: If animals had superhero costumes, these creatures would need the biggest capes.
The mantis shrimp punches with the speed of a speeding bullet.
Its punch can make the water flash and boil around it for a split second.
Mantis shrimp eyes can see colours that humans cannot even imagine.
The axolotl can regrow its own legs, heart, and even parts of its brain.
Scientists study axolotls hoping to unlock healing secrets for humans.
Tardigrades, tiny water bears, have survived the vacuum of space.
They can sleep through boiling, freezing, and crushing pressure for years.
The immortal jellyfish can restart its life cycle again and again.
When hurt or old, it melts back into a baby and starts over.
Electric eels can release shocks stronger than a household wall socket.
They use electricity to hunt, to defend, and to navigate dark rivers.
The archerfish shoots jets of water to knock insects off leaves.
It corrects for how light bends at the water's surface — pure physics.
Cheetahs can sprint faster than a car on a city street.
But a cheetah can only hold that speed for less than a minute.
The peregrine falcon dives faster than any other animal on Earth.
In a dive, it passes three hundred kilometres per hour.
Frogs that freeze solid in winter thaw out and hop away in spring.
The wood frog's heart stops all winter, yet it wakes up alive.
Sea cucumbers can eject their own insides to escape danger — and regrow them.
The mimic octopus impersonates other animals, from flatfish to sea snakes.
It is famous for copying many different creatures to stay safe.
Dung beetles navigate by the light of the Milky Way.
They are the first insects known to use the stars as a compass.
The pistol shrimp's snap creates a bubble that collapses with a flash of extreme heat.
Hippos sweat a pink fluid that works as natural sunscreen.
That pink sweat also fights germs on their skin.
The lyrebird can copy almost any sound — chainsaws, cameras, and other birds.
One lyrebird fooled a whole forest with perfect imitations.
Elephants communicate through rumbles so deep we feel them more than hear them.
Those rumbles travel through the ground for kilometres.
Bats find insects in total darkness using only echoes.
A bat's echolocation is so precise it can catch a moth in mid-flight.
The narwhal's famous tusk is actually a giant tooth full of nerves.
That tooth can sense the water around the whale like a living instrument.
Geckos climb glass using millions of tiny hairs on their toes.
Those hairs grip with the same forces that hold molecules together.
The bombardier beetle sprays boiling chemicals at its enemies.
It mixes the chemicals inside its body like a tiny living cannon.
Salmon return from the ocean to the exact stream where they were born.
They navigate using Earth's magnetic field and their sense of smell.
Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres across continents.
No single monarch makes the whole round trip — it takes generations.
The common swift can stay in the air for ten months without landing.
It eats, mates, and even sleeps while flying.
Camels can drink a hundred litres of water in ten minutes after a desert trek.
Their humps store fat, not water — nature's packed lunch.
Owls fly almost silently because of special soft edges on their feathers.
That silence lets them swoop on prey that never hears them coming.
The horned lizard can shoot blood from its eyes to confuse predators.
Nature invented this defence long before any comic book hero.
Starfish can regrow lost arms — and sometimes a whole body from one arm.
Spiders spin silk that is stronger, weight for weight, than steel.
Engineers study spider silk to design stronger ropes and cables.
From bullet punches to starlight compasses, animals out-invent our machines.
Every creature in this list is real, alive, and sharing our planet today.
The greatest superpowers were never in comics — they were in nature all along.
